Get-up-and-go means the natural energy, drive, and enthusiasm inside a person that pushes them to start things, take action, and keep going without needing someone else to push them. It is the inner force that gets a person moving — physically, mentally, and emotionally — toward doing things in life.

Think of it this way: some people wake up ready to tackle the day. They start projects, pursue goals, work hard, and stay motivated. Other people struggle to begin anything, feel drained, and need a push just to get started. The first type of person has get-up-and-go. The second type lacks it.
What It Really Means — Breaking It Down

The word captures three things at once, and it only truly means something when all three are present together:

1. Energy
This is the raw fuel — the physical and mental power that makes action possible. A person with get-up-and-go does not feel heavy, sluggish, or tired. They feel alive and capable.

2. Motivation
This is the desire to do things — the inner "want to." A person with get-up-and-go is not just capable of acting; they actually want to act. They are not waiting for someone to tell them what to do or why to do it.

3. Initiative
This is the willingness to start — to take the first step without being told, without waiting, and without hesitation. A person with get-up-and-go does not sit around wondering whether to begin. They simply begin.

When these three work together — energy + motivation + initiative — that is get-up-and-go. Remove any one of them and the word no longer fits perfectly. For example, a person might have the energy to run a marathon but no desire to do anything with their life. That is not get-up-and-go. Or a person might want to start a business but feels too exhausted and drained to ever take the first step. That is not get-up-and-go either.

Imagine the feeling you get on a day when everything clicks. You wake up early. You feel sharp. You look at your to-do list and instead of feeling overwhelmed, you feel ready. You jump into tasks. Hours pass and you have not slowed down. You feel alive, purposeful, and in motion. That feeling — that state of being — is what get-up-and-go refers to.

It is sometimes also called drive or vim or pep or gumption in English, but get-up-and-go captures something slightly broader than each of those words alone. It is a zest for doing things — for life itself.
How It Is Used — Presence and Absence

This word is used in two main ways: to describe someone who has it, and to describe someone who has lost it or lacks it.

When someone has it:

  • "She's full of get-up-and-go — she runs her own business, trains for marathons, and still volunteers on weekends."
  • "Even at 80, he had the get-up-and-go of a man half his age."
  • "You need real get-up-and-go to succeed in this industry."
  • "The new intern has great get-up-and-go — she is always the first to volunteer and the last to leave."

When someone lacks it or loses it:

  • "I used to have so much get-up-and-go, but lately I can barely start anything."
  • "Since he retired, he seems to have lost his get-up-and-go."
  • "She has the talent, but she just doesn't have the get-up-and-go to use it."
  • "I don't know what happened to me — I have no get-up-and-go these days."

Notice that the word works beautifully in both directions. Praising someone for having it and lamenting the loss of it are equally natural uses.

Get-up-and-go can describe any person at any age, but interestingly, it is especially common in two situations:

Praising an older person — When an elderly person is still energetic, active, and motivated, people often remark on their get-up-and-go because it surprises them. Age is expected to drain it, so when it persists, it stands out as admirable.

Praising a young, ambitious person — When a young person shows unusual initiative, drive, and hustle, people say they have real get-up-and-go, meaning they are not lazy or passive like others their age might be.

It can also describe a person at any stage of life who is notably energetic and self-driven compared to those around them.

There is a well-known joke in English that plays on the structure of this word:

"My get-up-and-go has got up and went."

This is intentionally grammatically incorrect (it should be "gone," not "went"), but that is part of the humor. It means: the energy and drive I used to have has completely left me. People — especially older adults — use this phrase in a self-deprecating, lighthearted way to say they feel tired, unmotivated, or past their prime. It is witty because it treats get-up-and-go as if it were a living thing that literally packed its bags and left.
What It Is NOT — Sharpening the Meaning

To understand a word fully, it helps to know what it does not mean:

  • It is not just physical energy alone. A person could be physically fit but unmotivated and passive — that is not get-up-and-go.
  • It is not just ambition alone. A person can dream of great things but feel too lazy or exhausted to pursue them — that is not get-up-and-go.
  • It is not stubbornness or aggression. A person with get-up-and-go is driven and enthusiastic, not pushy or forceful.
  • It is not always permanent. People can have get-up-and-go at one stage of life and lose it at another, due to illness, depression, burnout, age, or life circumstances.

This is an informal, everyday word. You would use it in conversation, casual writing, or a friendly context — not in a formal essay or professional report. It carries a warm, positive, and slightly admiring tone when used to describe someone. When used to describe a lack of it, it carries a tone of mild sadness, tiredness, or gentle humor.

Get-up-and-go is the quality a person has when they are naturally full of energy, motivation, and initiative — when they do not need to be pushed to take action, and they approach life with enthusiasm and drive.
